topic: Chemical cells and fuel cells (chemistry only)
subject: chemistry

items.q: A chemical cell is connected to a bulb and the bulb lights. Where does the electricity come from?
items.correct: From a reaction between the chemicals inside the cell
items.misconception: From electricity stored in the cell when it was made
items.why: Everyday language treats batteries as things that are full or empty, and diagrams of circuits show charge flowing out of the cell, which invites the picture of a tank being drained. Cells contain chemicals which react to produce electricity. Until the circuit is complete no current flows and no electricity exists in the cell; when the circuit is closed the reaction between the chemicals produces it.
items.random_wrong: From a supply of electrons held ready in the metal case

items.q: The voltage produced by a cell depends on a number of factors. Which of these is one of them?
items.correct: The type of metal used for each of the two electrodes
items.misconception: The size of the two pieces of metal used as electrodes
items.why: Students correctly learn that more reactant means more product, and wrongly transfer that quantity rule to voltage, which is not a quantity of anything produced. The factors named by the specification are the type of electrode and the type of electrolyte. Doubling the size of the electrodes does not double the voltage; a bigger cell may keep working for longer, but the voltage is unchanged.
items.random_wrong: How long the cell was stored away before its first use

items.q: A cell made from zinc and copper in copper sulfate solution gives 1.1 V. The copper sulfate solution is replaced by sodium chloride solution. What happens to the voltage?
items.correct: It changes, because voltage depends on the electrolyte used
items.misconception: It stays at 1.1 V, because the two metals are unchanged
items.why: The metals are the visible, obviously different parts of the cell, and students transfer the idea of a wire completing a circuit to the liquid, treating it as a passive connector. The specification states that the voltage is dependent upon a number of factors including the type of electrode and electrolyte. Both matter, so a cell with the same two metals in a different electrolyte can give a different voltage.
items.random_wrong: It stays at 1.1 V, because the electrodes are the same size

items.q: What is needed to make a simple cell?
items.correct: Two different metals in contact with an electrolyte
items.misconception: Two pieces of the same metal in contact with an electrolyte
items.why: The word 'electrode' is learnt from electrolysis, where two identical inert electrodes are normal, and that arrangement is carried over to cells without noticing the difference. A simple cell is made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte. Two identical electrodes have no difference in reactivity between them, so no voltage is produced.
items.random_wrong: Two different metals joined together by a length of wire

items.q: Which of these arrangements will produce a voltage?
items.correct: Zinc and copper strips dipping into sodium chloride solution
items.misconception: Zinc and copper strips dipping into a beaker of pure water
items.why: The liquid is seen as a way of joining the two metals, and water is the default liquid, so its role as a source of free-moving ions is overlooked. A simple cell is made by connecting two different metals in contact with an electrolyte. Pure water contains almost no free-moving ions; a salt solution such as sodium chloride solution is an electrolyte and works.
items.random_wrong: Two copper strips dipping into copper sulfate solution

items.q: What is a battery?
items.correct: Two or more cells connected in series to give a greater voltage
items.misconception: Another name for a single cell containing chemicals
items.why: Shops and everyday speech call every portable power source a battery, and the chemical meaning of the word is never encountered outside science lessons. Batteries consist of two or more cells connected together in series to provide a greater voltage. One cell on its own is a cell; joining cells in series makes a battery.
items.random_wrong: Two or more cells connected in series to give a greater current

items.q: Four identical 1.5 V cells are connected together in series to make a battery. What is the voltage of the battery?
items.why: Current is the quantity students picture flowing round the circuit, so 'more cells' is read as 'more flow', and series and parallel connection are easily confused. Cells are connected in series in a battery to provide a greater voltage. Four 1.5 V cells in series give a battery voltage of 6.0 V.

items.q: Why does a non-rechargeable cell eventually stop producing electricity?
items.correct: One of the reactants inside it has been completely used up
items.misconception: The store of electrons inside it has all been given out
items.why: It follows from the picture of a cell as a store of electricity, and the phrase 'the battery is dead' suggests something inside has been emptied rather than reacted. In non-rechargeable cells and batteries the chemical reactions stop when one of the reactants has been used up. Electrons are not consumed; they circulate. What runs out is a chemical reactant.
items.random_wrong: The electricity put in when it was made has been used up

items.q: Which statement about alkaline batteries is correct?
items.correct: They are non-rechargeable, so they cannot be recharged
items.misconception: They are rechargeable because they contain an alkali
items.why: Packaging uses 'alkaline' as a premium label, and students associate the extra cost and longer life with the rechargeable type they own. The specification is explicit: alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable. Once a reactant inside has been used up the reactions stop and supplying an external current will not reverse them.
items.random_wrong: They can be recharged by connecting a power supply

items.q: Why can a rechargeable cell be recharged?
items.correct: An external electrical current reverses the chemical reactions
items.misconception: An external current pushes fresh chemicals into the cell
items.why: Recharging is compared with refuelling a car, an analogy in which something material really is added, and nothing visible enters a battery to contradict it. Rechargeable cells and batteries can be recharged because the chemical reactions are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied. The same atoms are still in the cell; the products are turned back into the reactants.
items.random_wrong: An external current refills the cell's store of electrons

items.q: A rechargeable cell has gone flat and is connected to a charger. What happens inside the cell?
items.correct: The products of the reaction are turned back into reactants
items.misconception: New reactants are supplied to the cell through the electrodes
items.why: Recharging is compared with refuelling a car, an analogy in which something material really is added, and nothing visible enters a battery to contradict it. Rechargeable cells and batteries can be recharged because the chemical reactions are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied. The same atoms are still in the cell; the products are turned back into the reactants.
items.random_wrong: Electrical charge is stored between the electrodes for later

items.q: Cells are made using a copper electrode and a second metal in the same electrolyte. The voltages are: magnesium 2.7 V, zinc 1.1 V, iron 0.8 V, tin 0.5 V. What do these data show?
items.correct: The bigger the difference in reactivity, the bigger the voltage
items.misconception: Metals close together in the reactivity series give the biggest voltage
items.why: Students expect similar things to work well together, and 'close together' sounds like a stronger relationship than 'far apart'. The greater the difference in reactivity between the two metals, the greater the voltage. Two metals next to each other in the reactivity series give only a small voltage, and two of the same metal give none.
items.random_wrong: The heavier the second metal is, the smaller the voltage produced

items.q: A simple cell is made from magnesium and copper in an electrolyte. Which electrode is the negative one?
items.correct: Magnesium, because it is the more reactive of the two metals
items.misconception: Copper, because the less reactive metal releases the electrons
items.why: 'Positive' is read as a value word meaning better or stronger, and students match it to the more reactive metal instead of following the electrons. The more reactive metal loses electrons more readily, so it is the negative electrode. In a magnesium and copper cell magnesium is negative and copper is positive.
items.random_wrong: Whichever metal is the larger piece dipped into the liquid

items.q: Which statement is a valid reason for choosing a rechargeable battery instead of an alkaline battery?
items.correct: It can be recharged and reused, so less waste is produced
items.misconception: Alkaline batteries need recharging more often than it does
items.why: Packaging uses 'alkaline' as a premium label, and students associate the extra cost and longer life with the rechargeable type they own. The specification is explicit: alkaline batteries are non-rechargeable. Once a reactant inside has been used up the reactions stop and supplying an external current will not reverse them.
items.random_wrong: Recharging adds new chemicals, so it will never wear out

items.q: How is a hydrogen fuel cell kept working?
items.correct: Hydrogen and oxygen or air are supplied to it from outside
items.misconception: It is recharged from the mains when its fuel has run out
items.why: Fuel cells are met as an alternative to batteries and are pictured as batteries, so students assume the fuel must be stored inside like the reactants of an ordinary cell. Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel and oxygen or air. The fuel is fed in from outside, so the cell keeps working as long as the supply continues; it is refuelled, not recharged.
items.random_wrong: The hydrogen inside it is burned to heat the electrolyte

items.q: Which statement about the fuel in a fuel cell is correct?
items.correct: It is oxidised electrochemically, producing a potential difference
items.misconception: It is burned in oxygen, and the heat produced makes electricity
items.why: The word 'fuel' is tied to combustion in every other context students meet, from fuels in 4.7 to power stations, so a flame is assumed. The fuel is oxidised electrochemically within the fuel cell to produce a potential difference. The oxidation happens at an electrode, so the electrons pass through the external circuit instead of the energy being released as heat in a flame.
items.random_wrong: It is stored inside the cell and is used up as the cell works

items.q: What does the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell produce?
items.correct: Water, from the oxidation of hydrogen
items.misconception: Carbon dioxide, from burning fuel
items.why: The rule 'fuel plus oxygen gives carbon dioxide and water' is learnt for hydrocarbons and applied to hydrogen, which contains no carbon at all. The overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell involves the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water. Hydrogen contains no carbon, so no carbon dioxide can be formed: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
items.random_wrong: Hydrogen peroxide, from H₂ and O₂

items.q: Which equation shows the overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell?
items.correct: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O
items.misconception: H₂ + O₂ → H₂O₂
items.why: Formulae are built by carrying the subscripts of the reactants across into the product, instead of from the combining ratio of the elements. The formula of a compound comes from the combining ratio, not from the reactant formulae. Water is H₂O, and the balanced overall reaction is 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O.
items.random_wrong: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂

items.q: Which is an advantage of a hydrogen fuel cell over a rechargeable battery?
items.correct: It keeps working while fuel is supplied, with no recharging time
items.misconception: It can be recharged far more quickly than a battery can be
items.why: Fuel cells are met as an alternative to batteries and are pictured as batteries, so students assume the fuel must be stored inside like the reactants of an ordinary cell. Fuel cells are supplied by an external source of fuel and oxygen or air. The fuel is fed in from outside, so the cell keeps working as long as the supply continues; it is refuelled, not recharged.
items.random_wrong: It produces a much higher voltage than any battery can give

items.q: Which is a disadvantage of hydrogen fuel cells compared with rechargeable batteries?
items.correct: Hydrogen is difficult to store and to distribute safely
items.misconception: There are no disadvantages, so they will replace batteries
items.why: The single clean product is memorable and evaluation questions are answered by listing advantages only, so the other side of the comparison is never brought to mind. Hydrogen fuel cells offer a potential alternative to rechargeable cells and batteries. An evaluation must give both sides: no recharging time and water as the only product, set against the difficulty of storing and distributing hydrogen safely and the need for a hydrogen supply.
items.random_wrong: They release carbon dioxide from the cell as they work

items.q: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, which half equation shows the reaction at the negative electrode?
items.misconception: H₂ → 2H⁺ + e⁻
items.why: Balancing is first taught as balancing atoms, and electrons look like an optional extra written at the end rather than a species that must be counted. In a half equation the total charge must balance as well as the atoms. H₂ → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ has zero charge on each side; written with e⁻ it does not, and is wrong.

items.q: In a hydrogen fuel cell with an acidic electrolyte, which half equation shows the reaction at the positive electrode?
items.correct: O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O
items.misconception: 2H₂O → O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
items.why: The rule 'oxidation at the anode' is learnt in 4.4.3 together with 'anode is positive', and the pair is carried into fuel cells, where the electrode that supplies electrons to the circuit is the negative one. In a hydrogen fuel cell the hydrogen is oxidised at the negative electrode, 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, and oxygen is reduced at the positive electrode, O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O.
items.random_wrong: O₂ + 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ → 2H₂O

items.q: Can any flat cell be recharged if you connect it to a power supply?
items.correct: No. Only cells whose reactions can be reversed by the current are rechargeable.
items.misconception: Every cell can be recharged; you just need a charger, and the ones labelled non-rechargeable are labelled that way to make you buy more.
items.why: The mechanism of recharging is invisible, so 'putting the electricity back' seems like something that could be done to any cell. Recharging works only where the chemical reactions are reversed when an external electrical current is supplied. In a non-rechargeable cell such as an alkaline battery they are not, so it cannot be recharged.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: At the negative electrode of a hydrogen fuel cell, does hydrogen gain or lose electrons?
items.correct: It loses electrons: 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻.
items.misconception: The electrode is called negative, so electrons must be pushed onto the hydrogen there.
items.why: In electrolysis the negative electrode is where positive ions gain electrons, and that rule is transferred to a cell without noticing that in a cell the electrode is negative because the reaction there releases electrons. In a fuel cell the fuel is oxidised, and oxidation is loss of electrons. Hydrogen loses electrons at the negative electrode, 2H₂ → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻, and those electrons flow out into the circuit, which is what makes that electrode negative.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Do the cells in a battery share the total voltage between them?
items.correct: No. Their voltages add up to give a greater total.
items.misconception: The voltage of the battery is divided between the cells, so each cell in a four-cell battery only supplies a quarter of it.
items.why: Students meet potential difference sharing between components in series in physics and apply that rule to the sources rather than to the components. Batteries consist of two or more cells connected together in series to provide a greater voltage. Four 1.5 V cells in series give 6.0 V, not 0.375 V.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

items.q: Does a hydrogen fuel cell split water into hydrogen and oxygen?
items.correct: No. It does the opposite: hydrogen is oxidised to produce water.
items.misconception: A fuel cell is electrolysis of water, so water goes in and hydrogen and oxygen come out.
items.why: Fuel cells are taught close to electrolysis and both involve electrodes and hydrogen and oxygen, so the direction of the change is reversed in memory. The overall reaction in a hydrogen fuel cell involves the oxidation of hydrogen to produce water: 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O. Electrolysis of water is the reverse change and it consumes electricity instead of producing it.
items.note: no MCQ covers this misconception, so no third distractor was authored for it; none invented

specSource: AQA GCSE Chemistry (8462) specification; section 4.5.2 Chemical cells and fuel cells (chemistry only)
